name: Maximum Distributed Tree
description: You are given a tree that consists of $$$n$$$ nodes. You should label each of its $$$n-1$$$ edges with an integer in such way that satisfies the following conditions: each integer must be greater than $$$0$$$; the product of all $$$n-1$$$ numbers should be equal to $$$k$$$; the number of $$$1$$$-s among all $$$n-1$$$ integers must be minimum possible. Let's define $$$f(u,v)$$$ as the sum of the numbers on the simple path from node $$$u$$$ to node $$$v$$$. Also, let $$$\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n-1} \sum\limits_{j=i+1}^n f(i,j)$$$ be a distribution index of the tree. Find the maximum possible distribution index you can get. Since answer can be too large, print it modulo $$$10^9 + 7$$$. In this problem, since the number $$$k$$$ can be large, the result of the prime factorization of $$$k$$$ is given instead.
input_specification: The first line contains one integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 100$$$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 10^5$$$) — the number of nodes in the tree. Each of the next $$$n-1$$$ lines describes an edge: the $$$i$$$-th line contains two integers $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$ ($$$1 \le u_i, v_i \le n$$$; $$$u_i \ne v_i$$$) — indices of vertices connected by the $$$i$$$-th edge. Next line contains a single integer $$$m$$$ ($$$1 \le m \le 6 \cdot 10^4$$$) — the number of prime factors of $$$k$$$. Next line contains $$$m$$$ prime numbers $$$p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_m$$$ ($$$2 \le p_i \lt 6 \cdot 10^4$$$) such that $$$k = p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdot \ldots \cdot p_m$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases doesn't exceed $$$10^5$$$, the sum of $$$m$$$ over all test cases doesn't exceed $$$6 \cdot 10^4$$$, and the given edges for each test cases form a tree.
output_specification: Print the maximum distribution index you can get. Since answer can be too large, print it modulo $$$10^9+7$$$.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1401D — Maximum Distributed Tree [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
